questions.prompt:
An online furniture retailer introduced free returns last spring. Over the following six months, the share of its customers who made a second purchase rose from 22% to 31%. The retailer's marketing director concludes that free returns made customers more loyal.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the retailer's website displays customer reviews for each product
Whether customers prefer free returns to free delivery
Whether second purchases at online furniture retailers that did not introduce free returns also rose over the same period
Whether the retailer plans to extend free returns to its international customers
Whether returned items are resold at a discount
questions.explanation:
The director argues that free returns caused the rise in repeat purchases. The gap is that something else, such as a general market trend, may have caused it. (C) checks this with a comparison group. If repeat purchases rose just as much at retailers without free returns, the claim is weakened; if they did not, it is strengthened. Opposite directions, so it passes the variance test.

(A) concerns product reviews on the website, which have no clear bearing on whether free returns made customers more loyal. (B) compares two policies the argument doesn't compare. (D) concerns future plans. (E) concerns what happens to returned goods, not customer loyalty.
questions.tip: For causal arguments, look for the choice that asks what happened without the supposed cause.
questions.trap: (A) feels like a rival-cause question, but it only asks whether something happened, not whether it affected repeat purchases.

questions.prompt:
A gym manager says: "We asked members who attended our 6 a.m. spin class whether they were satisfied with the gym, and 94% said yes. Clearly, nearly all of our members are satisfied."

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether members who attend at other times of day are as satisfied as the 6 a.m. spin class members
Whether the gym has more members now than it had five years ago
Whether the 6 a.m. class is the most popular class at the gym
Whether the gym charges lower fees than competing gyms
Whether the spin instructors have professional qualifications
questions.explanation:
The manager generalises from one class to all members. The gap is whether the 6 a.m. spin attendees are representative. (A) asks exactly that: if other members are just as satisfied, the conclusion is supported; if they are much less satisfied, it is weakened. Opposite directions.

(B) concerns membership growth, which says nothing about satisfaction. (C) asks about popularity, which does not decide whether those attendees represent everyone. (D) is about price, not satisfaction among members. (E) concerns instructor credentials, which neither supports nor undermines the generalisation.
questions.tip: When a conclusion covers a whole group but the evidence comes from part of it, ask whether the part resembles the rest.
questions.trap: (C) sounds relevant because popularity feels like a measure of satisfaction, but it doesn't test whether the sample matches all members.

questions.prompt:
A telehealth service cut missed appointments in the province of Alpura by 30% after it began sending text reminders and offering video consultations. The health ministry of the neighbouring province of Borland plans to adopt the same service, expecting a similar fall in missed appointments.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether Alpura's telehealth service was more expensive than the service Borland plans to adopt
Whether most missed appointments in Alpura were by elderly patients
Whether patients in Alpura prefer video consultations to text reminders
Whether the causes of missed appointments in Borland, such as travel distance and forgetting, are similar to those that the service addressed in Alpura
Whether Borland has more doctors per person than Alpura
questions.explanation:
This is an analogy argument: what worked in Alpura will work in Borland. The key gap is whether Borland's problem has the same causes. (D) tests that. If Borland's missed appointments come from the same causes, the plan looks promising; if they come mainly from something the service does not address, it looks poor.

(A) concerns cost, not effectiveness. (B) asks about one age group in Alpura only, which does not compare the two provinces. (C) compares two features inside Alpura, not Alpura with Borland. (E) compares doctor numbers, which are not clearly tied to why patients miss appointments.
questions.tip: In analogy arguments, the useful question asks whether the two situations are alike in the way that matters.
questions.trap: (B) looks like a sampling question, but it studies Alpura alone, so it can't reveal whether the result transfers to Borland.

questions.prompt:
A bakery owner reasons: "Our single oven limits us to 400 loaves a day, and we sell out by noon every day. If we buy a second oven and double our output to 800 loaves, our daily profit will roughly double."

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the second oven would use more electricity than the first
Whether, once the bakery produces 800 loaves a day, it would still be able to sell the extra loaves at current prices
Whether the bakery's current oven is more than ten years old
Whether the bakery's loaves are priced above those of nearby supermarkets
Whether the owner has run another business in the past
questions.explanation:
The plan assumes the extra 400 loaves would sell at the same price. Selling out by noon shows demand at current output, but not at double. (B) tests this. If the extra loaves sell, profit may double; if they go unsold or need discounts, it will not. Opposite directions.

(A) is a cost detail that would affect profit only slightly and does not decide the main question. (C) concerns the age of the oven, not the plan. (D) is an interesting comparison, but price relative to supermarkets does not tell us whether demand extends beyond 400 loaves. (E) is about the owner's history.
questions.tip: For plan arguments, ask whether the plan's key step (here, selling double the output) is actually achievable.
questions.trap: (D) is attractive because pricing seems important, but the real question is about extra volume, not relative price.

questions.prompt:
A management consultant notes that employees at Datalink who take several short breaks during the workday produce 12% more output per hour than employees who take few breaks. She recommends that Datalink require all employees to take at least four short breaks daily to raise productivity.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the consultant has advised other companies on break policies
Whether the break-taking employees were already more productive before they began taking frequent breaks
Whether employees at other companies take more breaks than those at Datalink
Whether the short breaks at Datalink are paid
Whether output per hour is the best measure of productivity in every department
questions.explanation:
The consultant moves from a correlation (frequent breaks go with higher output) to a cause (breaks raise output). The gap is the reverse possibility: highly productive people may feel free to take breaks. (B) tests that. If they were already more productive, the recommendation is undermined; if not, it is supported.

(A) concerns the consultant's experience. (C) compares companies, not employees at Datalink. (D) concerns pay, which neither supports nor weakens the causal claim. (E) questions the measure, but it asks about every department, and a yes or no does not decide whether breaks cause higher output.
questions.tip: A correlation argument invites the question: which came first?
questions.trap: (E) sounds like a sharp critique of the evidence, but it targets the metric in general rather than the direction of cause.

questions.prompt:
A mid-sized insurer ran a six-month pilot of a four-day workweek in its claims department. The 60 employees who volunteered for the pilot processed 8% more claims per week than they had before it began. The chief executive proposes moving all 900 of the company's employees to a four-day week, expecting a similar gain in output across the company.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the volunteers' salaries were reduced during the pilot
Whether employees in other departments say they would like a four-day week
Whether other insurers have tried a four-day workweek
Whether the claims department is the largest department in the company
Whether the volunteers differ from the rest of the company's employees in ways that would make them especially likely to benefit from a shorter week
questions.explanation:
The CEO generalises from 60 volunteers to 900 employees. The gap is whether the volunteers are typical. (E) tests this: if they are typical, the expected company-wide gain is plausible; if they are unusually motivated or do unusually structured work, the gain may not repeat. Opposite directions.

(A) concerns pay, which is not tied to the output claim. (B) is tempting, but liking a schedule does not show that output will rise. (C) is about other companies. (D) concerns department size, which does not tell us whether the volunteers represent everyone else.
questions.tip: When a pilot is made of volunteers, ask how volunteers differ from everyone else.
questions.trap: (B) looks relevant because employee preference seems linked to productivity, but the CEO's claim is about output, not preference.

questions.prompt:
After a regional government ran a television campaign urging drivers to slow down, road fatalities in the region fell by 14% in the following year. The government's transport minister concluded that the campaign saved lives.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether fatalities in the region had, in earlier years, varied by as much as 14% from one year to the next without any campaign
Whether the television campaign cost more than earlier road-safety campaigns
Whether drivers who watched the campaign said they liked it
Whether the region has more roads than neighbouring regions
Whether the minister has previously supported road-safety measures
questions.explanation:
The minister assumes the fall was caused by the campaign. The gap is that fatalities may simply fluctuate from year to year. (A) tests that. If a 14% swing is normal, the fall tells us little (weakens); if it is unusual, the campaign looks effective (strengthens). Opposite directions.

(B) concerns cost. (C) concerns whether the campaign was liked, but a campaign can be liked and ineffective, or disliked and effective. (D) compares road networks, which says nothing about the fall in this region. (E) concerns the minister's history, not the evidence.
questions.tip: Before crediting a cause for a change, ask how big the change is compared with the normal ups and downs.
questions.trap: (C) feels connected to the campaign's impact, but approval is not the same as changed driving.

questions.prompt:
A business school reports that of the 62% of last year's graduates who responded to its placement survey, 91% had a job offer within three months of graduating. The school's director concludes that almost all of last year's graduates had a job offer within three months.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the school's graduates earn more than graduates of other business schools
Whether the school's fees have risen in the past five years
Whether the school has more applicants this year than last year
Whether graduates who did not respond to the survey were less likely to have received a job offer within three months than those who responded
Whether the job offers reported were for roles in the same industry as the graduates' previous jobs
questions.explanation:
The director moves from survey respondents (62%) to all graduates. The gap is non-response: people with good news tend to answer placement surveys. (D) tests that. If non-respondents were less successful, the conclusion fails; if they were as successful, it holds. Opposite directions.

(A) compares salaries, not the placement rate. (B) and (C) are about fees and applications, which do not bear on the 91% figure. (E) concerns the kind of job, but the claim is only about having an offer, so either answer leaves the conclusion where it was.
questions.tip: When only some people answer a survey, ask whether the people who did not answer are different.
questions.trap: (A) sounds like an indicator of placement success, but pay levels do not tell us how many graduates had an offer.

questions.prompt:
The national electricity regulator ran a pilot in which 5,000 households received smart meters that display real-time energy use. Over the first three months, these households used 9% less electricity than before. The regulator plans to install smart meters in all 20 million households and expects national household consumption to fall by about 9%.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the smart meters used in the pilot were installed by the same firms that will install them nationally
Whether households that received smart meters said they would recommend them to friends
Whether the households in the pilot continued to use less electricity after the first few months
Whether the cost of installing a smart meter exceeds the value of the electricity saved in three months
Whether the smart meters used in the pilot were made by a domestic manufacturer
questions.explanation:
The regulator extrapolates a three-month result to a permanent, national effect. The key gap is durability: the novelty of a new display may wear off. (C) tests that. If the saving persisted, the 9% projection is supported; if it faded, the projection is weakened.

(A) is a detail of logistics. (B) concerns satisfaction, which is not the same as continued savings. (D) is about cost-effectiveness, a different question from whether consumption falls by 9%. (E) concerns where the meters were made, which has no bearing on how much electricity households use.
questions.tip: When a short-term result is projected forward, ask whether the effect lasts.
questions.trap: (D) is tempting because it is a sensible business question, but the argument is about how much electricity is saved, not whether the scheme pays for itself.

questions.prompt:
Heartland Foods says that its new low-sugar breakfast cereal helps children avoid becoming overweight. In a trial, 200 children ate the cereal daily for a year, and only 8% of them became overweight, compared with 15% of children in the national school population over the same period.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the children in the trial usually ate the cereal with milk or with fruit
Whether the trial lasted longer than most nutrition studies
Whether the cereal contains more fibre than other breakfast cereals
Whether the parents of the children in the trial said they were satisfied with the cereal
Whether the children chosen for the trial were, before it began, less prone to gaining weight than children in the national school population
questions.explanation:
Heartland compares trial children with all children and credits the cereal. The gap is that the trial children may have differed from other children before the trial. (E) tests that: if they were less prone to weight gain (for example, from family diet or activity), the 8% figure is explained without the cereal; if they were similar, the cereal looks effective.

(A) concerns how the cereal is served, which has no clear link to the comparison. (B) is a comparison of study length, which does not decide whether the groups were alike. (C) concerns a possible mechanism but doesn't test the claim; the answer, yes or no, leaves the evidence unchanged. (D) is about parental satisfaction, unrelated to weight outcomes.
questions.tip: A comparison group only helps if it matches the test group before the test begins.
questions.trap: (C) invites you to find a reason the cereal could work, but explaining how it might work doesn't test whether it did.

questions.prompt:
Since a mandatory bicycle-helmet law took effect, the number of cyclists admitted to hospitals in the country with head injuries has fallen by 25%. The health minister claims that this shows that helmets protect cyclists from serious head injuries.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the law imposes fines on cyclists who do not wear helmets
Whether helmets are comfortable to wear in hot weather
Whether the number of people cycling in the country fell after the law took effect
Whether the minister has a background in medicine
Whether most cyclists admitted with head injuries before the law were commuters
questions.explanation:
The minister compares counts of head injuries, but the number of injured cyclists depends on how many people cycle. (C) tests this: if cycling fell sharply (perhaps because the law put people off), the fall in injuries may only reflect fewer cyclists, which weakens the claim; if cycling held steady or rose, the fall is more impressive, which strengthens it.

(A) and (B) are details of the law and the helmets that do not bear on the cause of the fall. (D) concerns the minister's qualifications, not the evidence. (E) is about the type of cyclist before the law, and neither answer would change whether helmets protect heads.
questions.tip: Counts can fall because the population exposed has shrunk; ask about the rate, not just the count.
questions.trap: (B) draws on a real-world concern but is irrelevant to whether the fall was caused by helmets.

questions.prompt:
A bike-share scheme launched in 2022 has been a success: usage rose from 2,000 trips a day to 9,000 trips a day. City officials conclude that the scheme is reducing car use in the city.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the scheme's fares are lower than public transport fares
Whether most trips taken on the bikes replace journeys that would otherwise have been made by car, rather than journeys on foot or by public transport
Whether the number of bike-share stations has grown at the same pace as trips
Whether bike-share users also own private bicycles
Whether the scheme was advertised on television
questions.explanation:
The officials infer less car use from more bike use. The gap is what the bike trips replaced. (B) tests it: if trips mostly replace car journeys, the conclusion is supported; if they mostly replace walking or buses, it isn't. Opposite directions.

(A) compares fares but doesn't say what travellers switched from. (C) concerns the scheme's size, not its effect on cars. (D) asks about a group that may be too small to matter, and neither answer tells us what the trips replaced. (E) concerns advertising, which has no bearing on substitution.
questions.tip: When a conclusion is about a substitute effect (X reduces Y), ask what X's users would have done otherwise.
questions.trap: (A) feels economic and relevant, but price alone doesn't show whether car users switched.

questions.prompt:
Orbit Telecom's analysts have found that customers who call the support line more than three times in a quarter are twice as likely to cancel their contracts as other customers. The analysts conclude that if Orbit cuts its average support-line waiting time from 14 minutes to 5 minutes, fewer customers will cancel.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether customers who go on to cancel their contracts had, on average, longer waits when they called the support line than customers who stay
Whether customers who call the support line more than three times in a quarter are charged for the calls
Whether the support line is staffed by employees who work in the same country as the customers
Whether customers who cancel their contracts mostly move to a single competitor
Whether customers who call the support line more than three times pay higher bills than other customers
questions.explanation:
The analysts move from a correlation (frequent callers cancel more) to a plan (shorter waits will reduce cancellations). The plan works only if waiting time itself contributes to cancelling. (A) tests that link directly: if future cancellers waited longer, shortening waits plausibly helps; if they waited no longer than other customers, shortening waits is unlikely to reduce cancellations. Opposite directions.

(B) and (E) concern call charges and bill size, which do not bear on whether waits cause cancellations. (C) concerns staffing location, which would matter only if it affected waiting time or quality, and the choice doesn't say so. (D) tells us where cancelling customers go, not why they leave; both answers leave the plan's logic untouched.
questions.tip: A plan built on a correlation needs the link between the lever you will pull and the outcome you want.
questions.trap: (B) and (E) are about the frequent callers, the group named in the evidence, which tempts you to pick them; but the plan concerns waiting time, not the group's characteristics.

questions.prompt:
The council of a large city wants to cut rush-hour congestion in the downtown core. Its analysts found that on days when the metro system suffers a delay of more than 20 minutes, road traffic into downtown rises by 18%. The council therefore plans to cut metro fares by 25%, reasoning that more commuters will take the metro and fewer will drive.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether metro delays of more than 20 minutes occur more often in winter than in summer
Whether drivers who commute into downtown would be more likely to switch to the metro if it were more reliable
Whether the metro's revenue would fall after the fare cut
Whether the people who drive into downtown on ordinary days cite metro fares as a main reason for not using the metro
Whether the 18% rise in traffic on delay days occurs mainly at rush hour
questions.explanation:
The delay evidence shows that existing metro users switch to cars when the metro fails. The plan, however, relies on regular drivers switching to the metro because of cheaper fares. (D) tests the plan's key step: if regular drivers are put off by fares, the cut should draw them in; if they are put off by something else, it will not. Opposite directions.

(B) is the strongest wrong answer. Reliability is a plausible lever, but the plan under evaluation is a fare cut, and (B) tests a different plan. (A) and (E) describe when delays and extra traffic occur but not what would move drivers. (C) is a financial question that doesn't affect whether congestion falls.
questions.tip: Test the plan actually proposed, not a better plan you might prefer.
questions.trap: (B) feels sophisticated because it follows from the delay evidence, but it evaluates reliability, not fares.

questions.prompt:
At Kestrel Ltd, employees who attended the company's voluntary time-management workshop last year received higher performance ratings, on average, than employees who did not attend. The human resources director concludes that the workshop improved employees' performance.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the workshop was held during working hours
Whether the workshop leader had written books on time management
Whether employees at other companies find time-management workshops useful
Whether the workshop was more expensive than the company's other training courses
Whether the employees who attended the workshop already received higher performance ratings than the others before they attended
questions.explanation:
The director credits the workshop for the higher ratings. The gap is that people who volunteer for a workshop may already be stronger performers. (E) tests this: if they were already rated higher, the workshop may have done nothing (weakens); if they were rated the same before, the workshop looks effective (strengthens).

(A) concerns scheduling, (B) concerns the leader's credentials, and (D) concerns cost. None changes what we conclude about the workshop's effect. (C) asks about other companies, which doesn't tell us what happened at Kestrel.
questions.tip: When a group chooses to take part, ask how it differed before taking part.
questions.trap: (C) sounds like evidence about workshops in general, but results at other firms don't show what caused ratings at Kestrel.

questions.prompt:
The owner of a café in a business district is considering extending its opening hours from 7 p.m. to midnight. She notes that a similar café two streets away, which has stayed open until midnight for years, earns 30% more per day than her café. She concludes that extending her hours will raise her daily earnings.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the café two streets away charges higher prices than hers
Whether her café's staff would be willing to work later hours
Whether there are enough customers in her neighbourhood after 7 p.m. to buy from a second café
Whether the café two streets away is older than hers
Whether the other café offers a larger menu
questions.explanation:
The owner assumes late-night customers exist in enough numbers for her café too. The gap is demand in the evening hours. (C) tests it: with plenty of late customers, extending hours should raise earnings; with few, she will pay for staff and lighting with no extra sales. Opposite directions.

(A) and (E) compare prices and menus, which could explain the other café's earnings but don't tell her whether longer hours would work. (B) is about practicality, and a yes or no on staff does not tell us whether hours raise earnings. (D) is about age, not demand.
questions.tip: A plan that copies a competitor needs the same conditions the competitor has.
questions.trap: (A) is a good-sounding explanation for the other café's advantage, but it doesn't tell us whether opening later brings customers.

questions.prompt:
In the year after the city planning office rezoned the Eastgate neighbourhood to allow taller buildings, the number of building permits issued there doubled. The office concludes that the rezoning stimulated new construction in Eastgate.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether the number of permits issued in Eastgate had been rising steeply in the years before the rezoning
Whether the new buildings in Eastgate are taller than those in other neighbourhoods
Whether residents of Eastgate supported the rezoning
Whether the planning office has rezoned other neighbourhoods
Whether permits in Eastgate are more expensive than in other neighbourhoods
questions.explanation:
The office treats the rezoning as the cause of the doubling. A rival explanation is an existing trend. (A) tests it: if permits were already rising steeply, the doubling may be a continuation (weakens); if they had been flat, the jump looks linked to the rezoning (strengthens).

(B) concerns building height, which doesn't show whether construction increased because of rezoning. (C) concerns local opinion. (D) asks about other neighbourhoods but not what happened in them. (E) concerns permit fees, which neither strengthens nor weakens the claim.
questions.tip: Before crediting an event for a jump, check whether the numbers were already climbing.
questions.trap: (D) looks like it could provide a comparison, but it asks whether rezoning happened elsewhere, not what happened to construction.

questions.prompt:
At Arden Corp, a software firm, switching to an open-plan office raised collaboration: the number of projects involving more than one team rose 40% within a year. The managing partner of Hale & Rao, a law firm, plans to adopt an open-plan layout, expecting a similar rise in collaboration among its practice groups.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether Arden Corp's employees preferred the open-plan layout to the old one
Whether Hale & Rao's office space is larger than Arden Corp's
Whether open-plan offices are cheaper to build than offices with walls
Whether the factors that limited collaboration among practice groups at Hale & Rao are the kind that an open-plan layout would remove
Whether Arden Corp is older than Hale & Rao
questions.explanation:
This is an analogy: what worked at Arden will work at Hale & Rao. The key question is whether the barrier to collaboration at Hale & Rao is the same as at Arden, namely physical separation. (D) tests this: if physical barriers were the issue, the plan looks promising; if the barriers are confidentiality rules or billing structures, an open plan won't help.

(A) concerns preference, not collaboration. (B) and (E) compare size and age, which do not address the cause of low collaboration. (C) concerns cost, which doesn't bear on the expected rise in collaboration.
questions.tip: For analogies, ask whether the barrier that the fix removed also exists in the new setting.
questions.trap: (A) feels relevant because happy staff might collaborate more, but it measures preference, not the effect on projects.

questions.prompt:
A study of 3,000 adults found that dog owners walked, on average, 40 minutes more per week than adults who did not own dogs. On the basis of this finding, a national health agency concludes that encouraging dog ownership would increase the amount of walking people do.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether dog owners in the study are, on average, younger than non-owners
Whether people who acquire a dog walk more after acquiring it than they did before
Whether dog owners in the study mostly walk in parks rather than on streets
Whether non-owners in the study walk less than the national average
Whether keeping a dog is expensive for most households
questions.explanation:
The agency moves from a correlation to a causal plan: encourage ownership to increase walking. The gap is whether getting a dog changes behaviour or whether people who already walk a lot choose to get dogs. (B) tests it. If people walk more after acquiring a dog, the plan works; if their walking is unchanged, ownership merely reflects existing habits and the plan fails. Opposite directions.

(A) is a possible confounder, but only one answer changes anything: if owners are younger, the claim weakens, but if they are not, we still don't know whether dogs cause more walking. (C) concerns where owners walk. (D) compares non-owners with the national average, which doesn't address cause. (E) concerns expense, a separate matter.
questions.tip: For a plan built on a correlation, look for the before-and-after test of the people the plan will change.
questions.trap: (A) is the tempting rival cause, but it is one-sided: a 'no' leaves the causal question open, while (B) settles it either way.

questions.prompt:
Between 2018 and 2023, the percentage of the workforce in the city of Marlow employed in manufacturing fell from 22% to 17%. The Marlow chamber of commerce concludes that Marlow's manufacturers have been shedding jobs.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether average wages in Marlow's manufacturing sector fell over the period
Whether other cities saw a similar fall in the share of their workforce employed in manufacturing
Whether jobs in Marlow's service sector pay more than jobs in its manufacturing sector
Whether manufacturing output in Marlow rose over the period
Whether Marlow's total workforce grew faster over the period than manufacturing employment in Marlow
questions.explanation:
The chamber infers a fall in the number of jobs from a fall in the share. The share can fall while the number stays the same or rises, if the total workforce grows faster. (E) tests this: if the workforce grew faster than manufacturing employment, the share would fall without job losses (weakens); if the workforce didn't grow that fast, jobs must have been lost (strengthens).

(A) concerns wages, not the number of jobs. (B) compares other cities, which doesn't tell us about Marlow's job numbers. (C) compares pay between sectors, which is off the point. (D) asks about output; output can rise with fewer workers, so either answer leaves the job-loss claim untouched.
questions.tip: A falling share does not prove a falling number; ask what happened to the total.
questions.trap: (D) is tempting because output sounds like the natural companion to jobs, but output can move either way without telling us whether jobs were cut.

questions.prompt:
A publisher wants to know whether releasing audio editions of all its titles would raise revenue. Six titles chosen at random from its catalogue were released in audio form last year, and sales of the audio editions equalled 35% of the print sales of those titles. The publisher concludes that releasing audio editions of all its titles would raise its total revenue by about 35%.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether audio editions cost more to produce than print editions
Whether audio editions of the six titles sold better in some countries than in others
Whether many buyers of the audio editions would otherwise have bought the print editions
Whether the six titles were released in audio form on the same date
Whether the publisher's audio sales have risen in each of the past five years
questions.explanation:
The publisher treats audio sales as pure additions to revenue. The gap is substitution: if audio buyers would have bought print copies, total revenue rises by far less than 35%. (C) tests this: if few would have bought print, the 35% estimate holds; if many would, the estimate collapses. Opposite directions. The titles were chosen at random, so representativeness is already covered.

(A) concerns production cost, but the conclusion is about revenue, not profit. (B) asks about geographic differences, which do not change the total. (D) concerns release timing. (E) concerns past trends in audio sales, which doesn't test whether the sales are additional.
questions.tip: When a new product is expected to add to sales, ask whether it takes sales from an existing product.
questions.trap: (A) feels like a business reality check, but the conclusion is about revenue, so costs are beside the point.

questions.prompt:
Researchers at the Brightwell Institute followed 5,000 retirees for ten years and found that those who volunteered at least four hours a week at the start of the study were 25% less likely to develop cognitive decline than non-volunteers. The researchers conclude that encouraging retirees to volunteer would reduce the rate of cognitive decline.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument above?
choices: Whether retirees who were in the early stages of undiagnosed cognitive decline at the start of the study were less likely to volunteer than other retirees
Whether the researchers received funding from organisations that rely on volunteers
Whether most volunteers in the study worked for charities rather than community groups
Whether the study would have shown the same result if it had followed the retirees for only five years
Whether the average age of the volunteers was higher than the national average age of retirees
questions.explanation:
The researchers want to credit volunteering, but the gap is reverse causation. Retirees in the early stages of decline might withdraw from activities like volunteering, which would create the same pattern without volunteering protecting anyone. (A) tests this: if early-decline retirees volunteered less, the finding is weakened; if they volunteered as often, the finding is strengthened.

(B) concerns funding, which would matter only if it affected the data. (C) concerns the type of volunteering, which doesn't test the cause. (D) is a hypothetical about a shorter study, and its answer would not tell us whether volunteering mattered. (E) compares the volunteers with all retirees nationally, which is the wrong comparison.
questions.tip: In long studies, ask whether the early stage of the outcome could have caused the supposed cause.
questions.trap: (D) looks like a sound methodological check, but a result from a shorter study would not reveal whether volunteering caused the outcome.

questions.prompt:
Every Brightline Tours employee who speaks Spanish was hired after 2020. Several of Brightline's tour guides speak Spanish, and all of its tour guides are employees.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: Most of Brightline's employees speak Spanish.
All of Brightline's tour guides were hired after 2020.
No employee hired before 2020 is a tour guide.
Several of Brightline's tour guides were hired after 2020.
Some employees hired after 2020 do not speak Spanish.
questions.explanation:
Several tour guides speak Spanish. Every Spanish-speaking employee was hired after 2020, and the guides are employees. So those same guides were hired after 2020, which makes (D) true. The word 'several' carries over.

(A) claims 'most employees', but we only know about guides. (B) says 'all' guides, but only the Spanish-speaking ones are covered. (C) is too strong: some guides who don't speak Spanish may have been hired before 2020. (E) assumes that some post-2020 hires lack Spanish, which the statements never say.
questions.tip: Follow each group through the chain; what the passage says about one group never automatically covers the larger group.
questions.trap: (B) extends a fact about Spanish-speaking guides to all guides.

questions.prompt:
Last year, Varna Airlines carried 4 million passengers, 60% of them on domestic routes. This year it carried 5 million passengers, 50% of them on domestic routes.

Which of the following can be properly concluded from the information above?
choices: The airline carried fewer international passengers this year than last year.
The airline carried more domestic passengers this year than last year.
The number of domestic passengers more than doubled.
The number of international passengers did not change.
Domestic routes became less profitable this year.
questions.explanation:
Work out the numbers. Last year: domestic 2.4 million, international 1.6 million. This year: domestic 2.5 million, international 2.5 million. Domestic passengers rose from 2.4 million to 2.5 million, so (B) is true even though the domestic share fell.

(A) is false: international passengers rose from 1.6 to 2.5 million. (C) is false: domestic passengers rose only slightly. (D) is false: international passengers rose. (E) brings in profit, which the passage never mentions.
questions.tip: A falling percentage doesn't mean a falling number; compute both years.
questions.trap: The falling share (60% to 50%) tempts you to say domestic passengers fell.

questions.prompt:
In a survey of 1,000 commuters in the city of Tarnow, most of those who cycle to work said they use public transport at least once a week. Few of those who drive to work said they use public transport weekly.

Which of the following can be properly concluded from the information above?
choices: A majority of commuters in Tarnow use public transport weekly.
Cycling to work makes people more likely to use public transport.
Most commuters in the survey cycle to work.
Few commuters who cycle to work own cars.
Commuters who cycle to work are more likely than commuters who drive to use public transport weekly.
questions.explanation:
Most cyclists use public transport weekly; few drivers do. So, in the survey, cyclists are more likely than drivers to use public transport weekly, which is (E).

(A) is unsupported: we don't know how many commuters cycle, so we can't say how many use public transport. (B) turns a correlation into a cause. (C) states a fact about how many cycle that the survey never gives. (D) brings in car ownership, which the passage doesn't discuss: cyclists may own cars.
questions.tip: A comparison of 'most' versus 'few' supports a safe 'more likely than' conclusion, and nothing stronger.
questions.trap: (B) adds a cause that the survey cannot support.

questions.prompt:
Between 2015 and 2023, the number of students enrolled in Halden University's MBA programme rose from 400 to 480, while the number enrolled in its undergraduate programmes fell from 6,000 to 5,400.

Which of the following can be properly concluded from the information above?
choices: The MBA programme's enrolment grew by a larger percentage than the undergraduate programmes' enrolment shrank.
The university's total enrolment in these two kinds of programme increased.
The MBA programme added more students than the undergraduate programmes lost.
Fewer than 5,000 students were enrolled in the university's undergraduate programmes in 2023.
The MBA programme is now larger than it has ever been.
questions.explanation:
MBA enrolment rose 80 students, or 20% (80/400). Undergraduate enrolment fell 600 students, or 10% (600/6,000). So the MBA's percentage growth (20%) was larger than the undergraduate decline (10%): (A).

(B) is false: the total fell from 6,400 to 5,880. (C) is false: the MBA added 80 while undergraduates lost 600. (D) is false: 5,400 undergraduates were enrolled in 2023. (E) is unsupported: earlier years are not given.
questions.tip: Convert to percentages before comparing growth and decline.
questions.trap: (C) compares percentages in the first sense and absolute numbers in the second; read which one each choice uses.

questions.prompt:
At Meridian Retail, women make up 40% of the company's 400 employees. The company's Finance department has 50 employees, and 80% of them are women.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: Most of the company's women work in the Finance department.
Finance is the largest department at the company.
Exactly one quarter of the company's women work in the Finance department.
Fewer than 100 of the company's women work outside Finance.
The Finance department has more male employees than female employees.
questions.explanation:
Women: 40% of 400 = 160. Finance women: 80% of 50 = 40. So 40 of the 160 women, exactly one quarter, work in Finance: (C).

(A) is false: only a quarter do. (B) is unsupported: other departments might be larger. (D) is false: 160 − 40 = 120 women work outside Finance, which is more than 100. (E) is false: Finance has 40 women and 10 men.
questions.tip: When percentages and totals are given, compute the counts rather than trusting how they sound.
questions.trap: (A) feels right because 80% is a big share, but it's 80% of a small department.

questions.prompt:
At the Dwarka outlet of a large furniture store, any item priced above ₹5,000 must be authorised by a manager before it can be sold. A manager never authorises a sale to a customer who has an unpaid balance with the store. Ravi has an unpaid balance with the store.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: Ravi cannot buy anything from the store.
Ravi's unpaid balance is larger than ₹5,000.
A manager authorises every sale above ₹5,000 to a customer who has no unpaid balance.
No customer with an unpaid balance has ever bought anything from the store.
Ravi cannot buy an item priced above ₹5,000 from the store.
questions.explanation:
Chain the rules. Items above ₹5,000 need manager authorisation. A manager never authorises a sale to someone with an unpaid balance. Ravi has one. So he can't get authorisation, and therefore can't buy an item above ₹5,000: (E).

(A) is too strong: cheaper items need no authorisation. (B) says the balance is large, but the passage gives no amount. (C) treats a necessary condition as a sufficient one; authorisation is required, not guaranteed. (D) overgeneralises: such customers can still buy items under ₹5,000.
questions.tip: A rule that requires something doesn't guarantee it; it only blocks sales when the requirement fails.
questions.trap: (A) extends a restriction on expensive items to all purchases.

questions.prompt:
Of the 120 companies listed on the Bexton stock exchange, 90 paid a dividend last year and 80 reported a profit.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: Exactly 50 companies both paid a dividend and reported a profit.
At least 50 companies both paid a dividend and reported a profit.
At least 60 companies both paid a dividend and reported a profit.
More than half of the companies that paid a dividend did not report a profit.
Every company that reported a profit also paid a dividend.
questions.explanation:
Use the overlap formula: 90 + 80 = 170, which exceeds the 120 companies, so at least 170 − 120 = 50 companies are in both groups. The overlap is at least 50, so (B) is true. (The overlap could be larger.)

(A) fixes the overlap at exactly 50, but it could be anything from 50 to 80. (C) sets a minimum above 50, which is not forced. (D) is false: at most 40 dividend payers (90 − 50) lacked a profit, which is fewer than half of 90. (E) is not forced: only 30 companies did not pay a dividend, and some of the 80 profitable companies could be among them.
questions.tip: Two groups whose sizes add to more than the total must overlap by at least the excess.
questions.trap: (B) mistakes the minimum overlap for the exact overlap.

questions.prompt:
On Beach Road, the Coral hotel is more expensive than the Dune hotel, and the Dune is more expensive than the Eden. The Fenwick is cheaper than the Dune but more expensive than the Grand. There are only five hotels on Beach Road.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: The Eden is more expensive than the Fenwick.
The Eden is more expensive than the Grand.
The Fenwick is more expensive than the Eden.
The Coral is more expensive than the Grand.
The Grand is the cheapest of the five hotels.
questions.explanation:
Write the orderings out. Coral > Dune > Eden. Dune > Fenwick > Grand. Coral > Dune > Fenwick > Grand, so Coral is more expensive than Grand: (D).

The Eden and the Fenwick are both below the Dune, but nothing relates them to each other, so (A) and (C) are unsupported. The Eden is related only to the Coral and Dune above it, so (B) cannot be confirmed. (E) isn't forced either: the Eden could be cheaper than the Grand.
questions.tip: Draw a quick ladder of the orderings; only links you can follow along a chain count.
questions.trap: (E) tempts because the Grand is the bottom of one chain, but the Eden's place relative to the Grand is unknown.

questions.prompt:
Most economists surveyed by the Financial Courier expect the central bank to cut interest rates in the next quarter. The bank's governor has said that no cut will be made unless inflation first falls below 4%. Inflation is currently 5.2%.

The statements above, if true, most strongly support which of the following?
choices: If the central bank cuts rates in the next quarter, inflation will have fallen below 4% before the cut.
Inflation will fall below 4% in the next quarter.
Most of the surveyed economists expect inflation to fall below 4% in the next quarter.
The governor's statement contradicts the economists' expectation.
A rate cut in the next quarter is impossible, given current inflation.
questions.explanation:
The governor's rule is a condition: no cut unless inflation is first below 4%. So if a cut happens, inflation must have dropped below 4% first: (A).

(B) predicts something the passage doesn't: the condition only applies if a cut happens. (C) attributes beliefs about inflation to the economists, which the passage doesn't say. (D) is too strong: inflation might fall quickly, so there is no contradiction. (E) is also too strong: inflation could drop below 4% within the quarter.
questions.tip: 'No X unless Y' means that if X happens, Y has happened; it predicts neither X nor Y.
questions.trap: (B) is tempting because it sounds like the governor's condition, but it runs the logic the wrong way.

questions.prompt:
At a certain university, 60% of the students are enrolled in a science programme. Of the students enrolled in a science programme, 70% are in their first or second year. Overall, 55% of the university's students are in their first or second year.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: More than half of the non-science students are in their first or second year.
Exactly 30% of the non-science students are in their first or second year.
Fewer than 35% of the non-science students are in their first or second year.
The proportion of non-science students in their first or second year equals that of science students.
At least 70% of the non-science students are in their first or second year.
questions.explanation:
Take 100 students. Science students: 60, and 70% of them (42) are in their first or second year. Overall, 55 students are in their first or second year, so 55 − 42 = 13 non-science students are in their first or second year. There are 40 non-science students, so 13/40 = 32.5% are in their first or second year. That is fewer than 35%: (C).

(A) is false: 32.5% is well under half. (B) is false: it is 32.5%, not 30%. (D) is false: 70% of science students are in their first or second year, against 32.5% of non-science students. (E) is false for the same reason: 32.5% is far below 70%.
questions.tip: Pick a convenient total, such as 100, and fill in the groups one at a time.
questions.trap: (B) is a rounded guess; the exact figure is 32.5%, so only the inequality is guaranteed.

questions.prompt:
Researchers in a call centre found that agents seated in the noisiest quarter of the floor handled fewer calls per hour than agents in the quietest quarter. After acoustic panels were installed in the noisy area, the average number of calls per hour handled by agents there rose by 6%.

The statements above, if true, most strongly support which of the following?
choices: Noise is the only factor that affects how many calls agents handle per hour.
Agents in the quietest quarter of the floor are more skilled than agents elsewhere.
Installing acoustic panels in the quiet area would raise call handling there by 6%.
Noise may be one of the factors that affects how many calls agents handle per hour.
Agents prefer working in quiet surroundings to working in noisy ones.
questions.explanation:
The evidence is consistent with noise affecting call handling: noisy desks had lower rates, and rates rose when noise fell. A cautious statement, using 'may be one of the factors,' is well supported: (D).

(A) says 'the only factor,' which the passage doesn't support. (B) asserts a difference in skill, which the passage doesn't mention. (C) predicts a 6% rise in a different area, but the quiet area may have no more noise to remove. (E) is about preference, which the passage doesn't measure: agents might be indifferent but still perform worse.
questions.tip: On 'most strongly supported' questions, the modest, hedged answer often beats the specific, confident one.
questions.trap: (A) overstates: evidence that something matters is not evidence that it is the only factor.

questions.prompt:
A company awards an annual bonus to an employee if, and only if, the employee's department meets its revenue target and the employee has no more than two unexcused absences during the year. Last year, Priya's department met its revenue target, but Priya did not receive a bonus.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: Priya's department was the only department to meet its revenue target last year.
Priya had at least three unexcused absences last year.
Priya's performance was below the average for her department.
Priya had more unexcused absences than any other employee in her department.
No one in Priya's department received a bonus last year.
questions.explanation:
'If, and only if' means both conditions are required and together enough. Priya's department met its target, so the revenue condition is satisfied. She still received no bonus, so the absence condition must have failed: she had more than two unexcused absences, which means at least three: (B).

(A) says nothing about other departments. (C) brings in performance, which plays no part in the bonus rule. (D) is a comparison with colleagues that the passage doesn't support: others might also have had more than two. (E) is wrong because other employees in her department with few absences would have received the bonus.
questions.tip: With an 'if and only if' rule, a failed outcome plus one satisfied condition points to the other condition failing.
questions.trap: (D) takes 'more than two absences' to mean 'the most absences', a step the rule doesn't support.

questions.prompt:
Historians have long attributed the decline of the port city of Veltria to the silting up of its harbour. However, municipal records show that the city's grain imports fell sharply about twenty years before the silting made the harbour unusable for large ships. The city's population began to fall during the same period as the fall in imports.

The statements above, if true, most strongly support which of the following?
choices: Grain imports fell because the city's population fell.
The city's decline was caused by something other than the state of its harbour.
The harbour was never important to the city's trade.
Historians were wrong to think that the harbour's silting had any role in the city's decline.
The harbour's becoming unusable for large ships cannot have been what first set the city's decline in motion.
questions.explanation:
Imports and population began falling about twenty years before the harbour became unusable for large ships. So that event came after the decline began, and cannot have started it: (E). The wording is narrow, about the harbour 'becoming unusable' and what first set the decline in motion.

(A) reverses the possible direction and isn't supported. (B) is too strong: the silting may have worsened the decline later. (C) is far too strong. (D) is also too strong: it denies any role, whereas the passage only dates the beginning.
questions.tip: Check the timing in the passage; an event that comes after something cannot have started it.
questions.trap: (B) and (D) are tempting because the passage challenges the historians, but they go beyond what the dates show.

questions.prompt:
Last year, the average salary of workers in a city's technology sector rose by 8%, and the average salary of workers in all its other sectors rose by 3%. The technology sector pays higher average salaries than the other sectors. The average salary of all of the city's workers rose by only 2%.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: The technology sector's share of the city's workforce fell last year.
The number of workers employed in the city fell last year.
Some workers outside the technology sector had their salaries cut last year.
Workers moved from the technology sector to other sectors last year.
The average salary in the technology sector is now lower than the average in other sectors.
questions.explanation:
The overall average is a weighted blend of the two sector averages. Each sector's average rose by at least 3%, so if the workforce mix had stayed constant, the overall average would have risen by at least 3%. It rose only 2%, so the mix must have shifted towards the lower-paying sectors: the technology sector's share fell: (A).

(B) is not needed: the total number can be anything. (C) is not forced: the average of non-tech workers rose 3%, which is consistent with no one's salary being cut. (D) is one way for the share to fall, but not the only way: non-tech employment could simply have grown faster. (E) is false: technology started higher and rose faster.
questions.tip: When every subgroup's average rises more than the overall average, the mix has shifted towards the lower-paid group.
questions.trap: (D) is plausible in real life, but the passage supports only that the share fell, not how it fell.

questions.prompt:
Every primary school in the town of Rosewood offers free lunches. Some of the town's schools are private. The Rosewood Academy is a primary school in the town.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: The Rosewood Academy is a private school.
All of the town's private schools are primary schools.
The Rosewood Academy offers free lunches.
Every school in the town offers free lunches.
No primary school in the town is private.
questions.explanation:
Every primary school in the town offers free lunches, and the Rosewood Academy is a primary school in the town, so it offers free lunches: (C).

(A) is unsupported: 'some' schools are private, but we don't know which ones. (B) reverses the claim about primary schools. (D) extends the rule from primary schools to all schools. (E) is also unsupported: a primary school could be one of the private schools.
questions.tip: Apply an 'every' rule only to the group it names.
questions.trap: (D) stretches the rule about primary schools to every school.

questions.prompt:
Over the past year, the share of Lumina's phone sales that came from its premium range rose from 20% to 25%, while the total number of phones Lumina sold fell by 10%.

Which of the following can be properly concluded from the information above?
choices: Lumina sold more premium phones this year than last year.
Lumina sold fewer premium phones this year than last year.
Lumina sold more non-premium phones this year than last year.
Lumina's non-premium sales fell by less than 10%.
Lumina's premium sales rose by 25%.
questions.explanation:
Use a base of 100 phones last year: 20 premium and 80 non-premium. This year Lumina sold 90 phones, of which 25% (22.5) were premium and 67.5 non-premium. Premium sales rose from 20 to 22.5, so (A) is true.

(B) is false for the same reason. (C) is false: non-premium sales fell from 80 to 67.5. (D) is false: the fall was about 15.6%, more than 10%. (E) is false: premium sales rose 12.5%, not 25%.
questions.tip: Pick a round base number and compute both years.
questions.trap: (B) is a trap for people who see total sales falling and assume every part fell.

questions.prompt:
A grants committee requires every research proposal to be endorsed by a department head or to include a budget under ₹10 lakh. Dr Menon's proposal, which includes a budget of ₹15 lakh, was submitted to the committee and accepted. It showed no evidence of prior pilot work.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: The committee rejected the proposal at first.
Dr Menon's proposal included evidence of prior pilot work.
Every proposal with a budget above ₹10 lakh was endorsed by a department head.
Every proposal with a budget under ₹10 lakh was endorsed by a department head.
A department head endorsed Dr Menon's proposal.
questions.explanation:
The committee's requirement is that every proposal be endorsed or have a budget under ₹10 lakh. Dr Menon's proposal was accepted, so it met the requirement. Its budget (₹15 lakh) is not under ₹10 lakh, so it must have been endorsed by a department head: (E).

(A) is unsupported. (B) is contradicted by the passage. (C) overgeneralises from one proposal to all large-budget proposals. (D) is wrong because proposals under ₹10 lakh satisfy the requirement without endorsement.
questions.tip: With an 'either/or' requirement, if one option is ruled out for a case, the other must hold.
questions.trap: (C) generalises from the one proposal we know about to all proposals above ₹10 lakh.

questions.prompt:
Five speakers (Bose, Mehta, Nair, Rao and Singh) each gave one talk at a conference, one after another, with no two talks at the same time. Mehta spoke before Rao, and Rao spoke before Singh. Singh did not give the last talk. Nair did not give the first talk.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: Mehta gave the first talk.
Either Nair or Bose spoke after Singh.
Singh gave the fourth talk.
Bose spoke after Rao.
Nair spoke after Rao.
questions.explanation:
Mehta, Rao and Singh speak in that order. Singh is not last, so someone speaks after Singh. The only speakers not already placed before Singh are Nair and Bose, so one of them speaks after Singh: (B).

(A) is not forced: Bose could speak first. (C) is not forced: Singh could be third, with Nair and Bose both after. (D) is not forced: Bose could be first. (E) is not forced: Mehta, Nair, Rao, Singh, Bose is a valid order in which Nair speaks before Rao.
questions.tip: Place the fixed chain first, then see what the remaining people can do.
questions.trap: (A) feels natural because Mehta starts the chain, but another speaker may precede him.

questions.prompt:
The town council of Alderley reports that recorded burglaries fell by 20% in the year after it installed street lighting in the town centre. The report also notes that the number of burglaries recorded by the police had fallen in each of the five years before the lighting was installed.

The statements above, if true, most strongly support which of the following?
choices: Street lighting reduces burglaries in town centres.
The police were less effective at recording burglaries after the lighting was installed.
The number of burglaries actually committed in Alderley fell by 20% after the lighting was installed.
The fall in recorded burglaries after the lighting was installed continued a downward trend that had begun earlier.
Street lighting had no effect on the number of burglaries in Alderley.
questions.explanation:
Recorded burglaries fell in each of the five years before the lighting and fell again by 20% after it. So the post-lighting fall continued an existing trend: (D).

(A) is a general causal claim that the passage can't support, since the trend was already under way. (B) invents a change in police practice. (C) confuses recorded burglaries with burglaries actually committed. (E) goes too far the other way: the lighting may have contributed to the fall without being its only cause.
questions.tip: Notice whether a passage gives you recorded figures or actual figures; they are not the same thing.
questions.trap: (A) and (E) both leap to a verdict about the lighting; the safer inference is only that the fall fits a prior trend.

questions.prompt:
A study of 2,000 adults over 60 found that those who reported regularly doing crossword puzzles scored higher on a memory test than those who did not. The study's authors noted that the participants who did crosswords regularly also had, on average, more years of formal education than the others.

The statements above, if true, most strongly support which of the following?
choices: Doing crossword puzzles improves memory in adults over 60.
Education, rather than crossword puzzles, explains the higher memory scores.
The difference in memory scores between the two groups may be due in part to the difference in their education.
People who do crosswords regularly score higher on memory tests than they did before they began doing crosswords.
Formal education improves memory in adults over 60.
questions.explanation:
The authors flag a second difference between the groups, education. That leaves open the possibility that education accounts for part of the memory difference: (C), stated with the cautious 'may be due in part.'

(A) claims a cause that the study's design cannot establish. (B) swings too far the other way: it says education, not crosswords, explains the scores, which excludes a role for crosswords. (D) is about before-and-after change, which the study never measured. (E) claims a cause for education that the passage doesn't test.
questions.tip: When a passage mentions a second difference between groups, the safe inference is that the difference may be part of the explanation.
questions.trap: (B) is tempting because it flips (A), but it denies any role for crosswords, which the passage doesn't.

questions.prompt:
In a poll of 500 voters, 60% said they support a new transport tax. The sample contained exactly 300 car owners, and 35% of the car owners in the sample said they support the tax.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: Fewer than half of the non-car-owners in the sample support the tax.
Exactly 90% of the non-car-owners in the sample support the tax.
Most of the supporters in the sample are car owners.
The tax is supported by more car owners than non-car-owners in the sample.
More than 95% of the non-car-owners in the sample support the tax.
questions.explanation:
Supporters: 60% of 500 = 300. Car-owner supporters: 35% of 300 = 105. Non-car-owners: 500 − 300 = 200, and supporters among them: 300 − 105 = 195. 195/200 = 97.5%, which is more than 95%: (E).

(A) is false: 97.5% is almost all. (B) is false: it is 97.5%, not exactly 90%. (C) is false: only 105 of the 300 supporters own cars. (D) is false: 105 car owners support against 195 non-car-owners.
questions.tip: Convert each percentage to a head-count; the missing group is what's left over.
questions.trap: (B) is a rounded guess; always compute the exact figure before choosing a numerical claim.

questions.prompt:
A company's hiring policy has these features. No applicant who failed the aptitude test was interviewed unless a director vouched for the applicant. Every applicant who was hired was interviewed. Mira was hired, and no director vouched for her.

Which of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?
choices: Mira's aptitude test result was among the highest of all the applicants'.
Mira did not fail the aptitude test.
Every applicant who passed the aptitude test was interviewed.
A director vouched for every applicant who failed the aptitude test.
Mira was not interviewed.
questions.explanation:
Chain the rules backwards. Mira was hired, so she was interviewed. Failing applicants were interviewed only if a director vouched for them, and none vouched for Mira. So Mira cannot have failed: (B).

(A) says too much: passing doesn't mean a top result. (C) reverses the rule, which restricts failed applicants only. (D) reverses the rule too: vouching was a requirement for failers to be interviewed, not a promise to vouch for all of them. (E) contradicts the second statement.
questions.tip: Work backwards from the outcome through each rule and ask what had to be true.
questions.trap: (A) is an enticing 'must have done well' story, but the rule is only about failing versus passing.

questions.prompt:
A small-town cinema began offering cheaper tickets on Tuesdays. Attendance on Tuesdays rose sharply. Yet the cinema's total attendance for the week did not change.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The cinema is closed on Mondays.
Many customers who had previously come on other days of the week switched to Tuesdays to get the lower price.
The cinema's Tuesday tickets are cheaper than tickets at other cinemas in the town.
The cinema showed several new films on Tuesdays.
Total attendance at the town's other cinemas fell during the same period.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: attendance rose on Tuesdays but the weekly total was flat. If Tuesday's extra viewers simply moved from other days, both facts are true: (B).

(A) is irrelevant to Tuesday versus the rest. (C) compares prices with other cinemas, which doesn't explain the flat total. (D) might explain a Tuesday rise, but would, if anything, make the total rise too, so it leaves the flat total unexplained. (E) concerns other cinemas and tells us nothing about this cinema's week.
questions.tip: When a part rises but the whole is flat, look for movement between parts.
questions.trap: (D) explains only half of the puzzle, the Tuesday rise, and does nothing for the flat weekly total.

questions.prompt:
The city of Raintree has more public libraries per head of population than any other city in its region. Yet its residents borrow fewer books per head than residents of any other city in the region.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Raintree's libraries also lend e-books.
Residents of Raintree read more books than residents of other cities in the region.
Libraries in other cities in the region charge fines for late returns.
The population of Raintree has grown in recent years.
Most of Raintree's libraries are small branches that stock only a few hundred books and open for only a few hours a week.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: lots of libraries, little borrowing. If most of the libraries are tiny and open rarely, then having many libraries doesn't give residents much access: (E).

(A) would raise borrowing, which deepens the puzzle (and e-books may not count as borrowed books). (B) makes the puzzle worse: more reading with fewer loans is harder to explain. (C) concerns other cities' practices, not Raintree's. (D) is irrelevant: population growth doesn't explain why borrowing per head is low.
questions.tip: Look for a reason why the first fact (many libraries) doesn't produce the expected effect.
questions.trap: (B) sounds like a reason to borrow fewer books (people buy their own), but it isn't stated, and it contradicts the 'read more' framing.

questions.prompt:
Over the past decade, the percentage of Delmar's adults who smoke has fallen steadily. Yet over the same decade, the number of smokers in Delmar has risen.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The price of cigarettes in Delmar has risen.
Many smokers in Delmar say that they want to quit.
Delmar's adult population has grown faster than the percentage of adults who smoke has fallen.
Smokers in Delmar now smoke fewer cigarettes per day than they used to.
The government of Delmar has run several anti-smoking campaigns.
questions.explanation:
This is the percent-versus-number pattern. If the adult population grows enough, a smaller percentage of a much larger group can be a bigger number: (C).

(A) and (E) give reasons for smoking to fall, which deepens the puzzle. (B) is about intentions, not numbers. (D) concerns how much each smoker smokes, not how many smokers there are.
questions.tip: When a percentage and a count move in opposite directions, check what happened to the total.
questions.trap: (D) is plausible in the real world but is silent on the number of smokers.

questions.prompt:
Last year, a manufacturer's profit per unit sold rose substantially. Yet the manufacturer's total profit for the year fell.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: To raise its margins, the manufacturer stopped selling its cheapest models, which had accounted for most of its sales volume.
The manufacturer cut its advertising spending.
The manufacturer's competitors also raised their profit per unit.
Raw material prices fell during the year.
The manufacturer's profit per unit was lower than that of its competitors.
questions.explanation:
Total profit = profit per unit × units sold. For profit per unit to rise while total profit falls, units sold must have fallen by more. (A) supplies the reason: dropping the cheap, high-volume models raised the average margin but cut the volume sharply.

(B) would help profit rise, not fall. (C) is about competitors and doesn't explain the manufacturer's total. (D) would raise profit per unit and so deepens the puzzle. (E) compares with competitors, which does nothing for the clash.
questions.tip: Split a total into rate times quantity and ask which one could have moved the other way.
questions.trap: (D) explains why per-unit profit rose, which is already given, and ignores the fall in total.

questions.prompt:
A software company reported that its subscription revenue rose 15% in the latest quarter. Yet the company's cash balance at the end of the quarter was lower than at the start.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The company recognises its subscription revenue monthly.
Most of the company's customers renewed their subscriptions.
Competitors of the company lost subscribers during the quarter.
During the quarter, the company paid a large sum to acquire another firm.
The company's share price rose during the quarter.
questions.explanation:
Revenue up, cash down. Something must have taken cash out: a large acquisition payment explains it: (D).

(A) describes an accounting approach, not a drain on cash. (B) and (C) would support revenue growth, deepening the puzzle. (E) is about the share price, which doesn't change a company's cash.
questions.tip: Ask which fact needs the explanation; here it is the fall in cash.
questions.trap: (B) explains why revenue rose, which isn't the puzzle.

questions.prompt:
A company's departments are Sales, Support and Logistics. This year, the average salary in each of the three departments is higher than it was last year. Yet the company-wide average salary is lower than it was last year.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The company gave large raises to its senior executives.
The company hired many new employees in its lowest-paying department.
The company's total payroll rose this year.
The average salary in Sales rose more than in the other departments.
The rate of inflation rose this year.
questions.explanation:
If every department's average rose but the overall average fell, the mix of employees must have shifted towards the lower-paid group. Hiring many new employees into the lowest-paying department does this: (B).

(A) would push the company average up. (C) is about total payroll, which can rise while the average falls but doesn't explain it. (D) says which department's average rose most, which doesn't alter the mix. (E) is irrelevant: inflation would raise salaries, not lower the overall average.
questions.tip: When subgroup averages all rise but the overall average falls, look for a shift in mix.
questions.trap: (C) sounds like a pay story but a bigger payroll is consistent with either outcome.

questions.prompt:
In a clinical trial, patients taking the new drug Cardiox suffered fewer heart attacks than patients taking a placebo. Yet more patients taking Cardiox died during the trial than patients taking the placebo.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many of the patients in the trial had a history of heart disease.
Heart attacks occurred in both groups.
Cardiox is cheaper than comparable drugs.
Many patients taking Cardiox stopped taking it before the trial ended.
Cardiox increases the risk of fatal strokes and other conditions by more than it reduces the risk of fatal heart attacks.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: the drug reduces heart attacks but more patients on it died. A reason why Cardiox could cause more deaths from other causes than it prevents resolves the clash: (E).

(A) and (B) describe features of the groups that are equally true of both. (C) concerns cost, not mortality. (D) would make the groups more alike, but would not make deaths higher in the Cardiox group.
questions.tip: A discrepancy about totals often needs a second effect, a side effect or a hidden cause that goes the other way.
questions.trap: (D) feels like a trial-quality problem, but it would shrink differences rather than reverse them.

questions.prompt:
Kavi's café raised its price for a cup of coffee by 15%. Over the following month, the number of cups of coffee it sold per day rose.

Each of the following, if true, helps to explain the rise in sales EXCEPT:
choices: A competing café a few doors away closed down at about the time Kavi raised prices.
A large new office building opened nearby, bringing hundreds of workers to the area.
Many of Kavi's regular customers told the staff that they found the new prices too high.
Kavi's café began giving a free pastry with every cup of coffee.
Kavi's café introduced a new coffee blend that quickly became popular.
questions.explanation:
Four of the choices give a reason why more coffee would be sold despite the higher price. The exception is the one that does nothing to explain a rise.

(C) is the exception: customers saying the prices are too high would, if anything, make a sales rise harder to understand, so it does not help. (A) removes a competitor, sending customers to Kavi. (B) brings in new customers. (D) offsets the higher price with a free item. (E) adds a popular product that pulls in customers.
questions.tip: On EXCEPT questions, test each choice as 'helps' or 'doesn't help', and pick the one that doesn't, even if it deepens the puzzle.
questions.trap: The EXCEPT stem flips your usual job; (C) feels like a natural 'reason' but works against the explanation.

questions.prompt:
The population of a rare bird species living on a remote island fell sharply after a conservation group removed an invasive species of rat that had preyed on the birds' eggs.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: After the rats were removed, feral cats that had previously fed mainly on the rats began to feed on the birds.
Removing the rats from the island was expensive.
The birds also feed on insects found on the island.
Rats on neighbouring islands have not been removed.
The birds lay their eggs on the ground.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: removing a predator should help the birds, but their numbers fell. A new predator that was kept in check by the rats now preys on the birds: (A) lets both be true.

(B) is about cost and doesn't affect the birds. (C) is irrelevant. (D) concerns other islands. (E) describes a vulnerability that existed both before and after the removal, so it doesn't explain the change.
questions.tip: Removing one problem can unlock another; look for a knock-on effect.
questions.trap: (E) seems to explain egg loss but applied equally before the rats left.

questions.prompt:
Between 2015 and 2023, the number of patents granted to Sundar Corp rose by 40%. Over the same period, Sundar's annual spending on research and development fell by 10%.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Several of Sundar's competitors were also granted more patents in that period.
Sundar's research staff were paid more in 2023 than in 2015.
Sundar's marketing spending rose between 2015 and 2023.
