Patents granted in a given year generally result from research carried out several years earlier, and Sundar had greatly increased its research spending in the years before 2015.
Sundar's patents are valid for twenty years.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: more patents, less spending. Patents usually come years after the research. If Sundar spent heavily before 2015, the patents granted in 2015-2023 can reflect that earlier spending: (D). This is the different-time-periods pattern.

(A) concerns competitors. (B) would raise spending, deepening the puzzle. (C) concerns marketing, not patents. (E) concerns how long patents last, not how many are granted.
questions.tip: When an outcome and its cause move in opposite directions, check whether they are measured at different times.
questions.trap: (A) offers a general trend among competitors but gives no reason why Sundar's patents should rise as its spending falls.

questions.prompt:
After a city opened a bus-only lane on its main avenue, the average time buses took to travel along the avenue fell. Yet the average time that bus passengers spent travelling from their starting point to their destination rose.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: More people began to travel by bus after the lane opened.
Fares for bus journeys on the avenue did not change.
To use the bus-only lane efficiently, the transport company cut the number of stops on the avenue, so many passengers now walk farther to reach a stop or change buses.
Fewer cars used the avenue after the bus lane opened.
Buses on the avenue are cleaner than they were before the lane opened.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: buses got faster on the avenue, but passengers' total journey time rose. Journey time includes more than time on the bus. If the bus company cut stops, passengers now spend more time walking or changing buses: (C).

(A) says nothing about journey time. (B) concerns fares. (D) would, if anything, speed up all traffic, deepening the puzzle. (E) concerns cleanliness and has no connection with time.
questions.tip: A total (door-to-door time) can rise even when one part (time on the bus) falls; look for the part that grew.
questions.trap: (A) sounds like it could cause crowding and delays, but nothing says it does.

questions.prompt:
A pharmaceutical firm's best-selling painkiller was withdrawn from the market after safety concerns. In the following year, the firm's total profit rose.

Each of the following, if true, helps to explain the rise in profit EXCEPT:
choices: Many customers who had bought the withdrawn painkiller switched to the firm's other painkillers, which carry higher margins.
The firm had been spending heavily on advertising the withdrawn painkiller, and stopped.
The firm raised the prices of its remaining products.
The firm received a large payment from selling the rights to one of its other drugs.
The withdrawn painkiller had accounted for most of the firm's profit in the previous year.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle is why profit rose even though the main product was withdrawn. Four choices explain it. (A) shifts sales to higher-margin products. (B) removes a big cost. (C) raises prices on what remains. (D) adds a one-off income.

(E) is the exception: if the withdrawn painkiller had provided most of the profit, losing it should have made profit fall, which deepens the puzzle rather than helping to explain it.
questions.tip: On EXCEPT questions, the odd one out is often the choice that strengthens the reason to expect the opposite.
questions.trap: (B) can look like an irrelevant cost story, but it is a genuine explanation; the real exception is (E).

questions.prompt:
Over the past decade in the country of Valdria, the proportion of university graduates who find jobs within six months of graduating has risen steadily. Yet over the same decade, surveys show that the proportion of employers who say they are satisfied with the skills of new graduates has fallen.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The number of universities in Valdria increased during the decade.
As the economy grew faster than the number of graduates, employers began to hire graduates with weaker skills whom they would earlier have turned down.
Employers' surveys in Valdria are conducted by post.
Starting salaries for graduates in Valdria rose during the decade.
Graduates in Valdria now apply for more jobs than they used to.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: more graduates are being hired, but employers are less satisfied. If demand for graduates outstripped supply, employers would have lowered their standards to fill jobs, hiring graduates they once rejected. That raises the hiring rate and lowers average satisfaction: (B).

(A) suggests more graduates, which might lower quality, but gives no reason why the job rate would rise. (C) is irrelevant. (D) fits a strong job market but says nothing about satisfaction. (E) might raise the hiring rate, but not employers' dissatisfaction.
questions.tip: A single hidden factor (here, a tight labour market) can push two measures in opposite directions.
questions.trap: (A) explains one side only (graduate quality) but does nothing about the rising employment rate.

questions.prompt:
A regional bank introduced a rule that loan officers' bonuses depend on the proportion of their loans that are repaid on time. After the rule took effect, the proportion of the bank's loans that were repaid on time rose substantially. Yet the share of the money the bank lent that it ultimately failed to recover also rose.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Loan officers shifted towards making many small loans that are nearly always repaid on time, while the loans that were not repaid tended to be very large.
Loan officers received larger bonuses after the rule took effect.
Interest rates in the region rose during the period.
The average income of the bank's borrowers rose during the period.
The bank's total lending increased during the period.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: a higher share of loans repaid on time, yet a higher share of money lost. The first measure counts loans; the second counts money. If officers piled up small safe loans (which lift the on-time share by number) while the few non-repaid loans were large (which drive money lost), both are true: (A).

(B) is about bonuses, which doesn't explain the losses. (C) could raise losses but wouldn't explain why the on-time proportion rose. (D) would reduce losses, deepening the puzzle. (E) concerns total lending, but the discrepancy is about shares, which are unaffected by scale.
questions.tip: Compare what each measure counts (number of loans or amount of money); different measures can diverge.
questions.trap: (C) explains the rise in losses but not the improved on-time share; always check both facts.

questions.prompt:
Last year, the average price of electric cars in the country fell sharply. Yet last year, sales of electric cars in the country fell.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Petrol cars were more popular than electric cars in the country last year.
Electric cars are made by fewer manufacturers than petrol cars.
Charging stations are more common in cities than in villages.
A government subsidy for buyers of electric cars was abolished at the start of last year, raising the net cost to buyers.
The country imports most of its electric cars.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: prices fell, but sales fell. If a subsidy was withdrawn, buyers' net cost may have risen even though sticker prices fell: (D).

(A) is a comparison with petrol cars that was true all along and so cannot explain a change. (B), (C) and (E) describe general facts about the market that do not relate to why sales fell last year.
questions.tip: When the expected cause (lower prices) doesn't give the expected effect, look for a change in the real cost or demand.
questions.trap: (A) sounds like a reason people buy fewer electric cars, but it describes the usual state, not a change.

questions.prompt:
After a firm introduced a work-from-home option, employees who worked from home reported higher job satisfaction than before. Yet the firm's employee turnover rose over the following year.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Working from home made it easier for employees to take jobs with employers based in other cities.
Employees who work from home spend less time commuting.
The firm's pay scales remained unchanged during the year.
The firm's satisfaction surveys were answered anonymously.
The firm's office is located in the centre of the city.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: happier staff, but more leaving. If working from home let people take jobs with distant employers, employees could be satisfied with their working arrangement and still leave for other opportunities: (A).

(B) is a further reason to be satisfied and so deepens the puzzle. (C) rules out a pay change, which does not explain the departures. (D) concerns the survey method, not turnover. (E) is irrelevant.
questions.tip: Satisfaction with one thing doesn't prevent people from leaving for another.
questions.trap: (B) is a nice-to-have of working from home, but it explains satisfaction, not turnover.

questions.prompt:
After a national park abolished its entrance fee, the number of visitors to the park doubled. Yet the total amount that visitors spent in the nearby town fell.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The park's entrance fee had been among the lowest of any national park in the country.
Park rangers reported that litter in the park increased after the fee was abolished.
The nearby town has more hotels than any other town in the region.
Many of the new visitors come from the surrounding region.
Before the fee was abolished, most visitors stayed overnight in the town's hotels; many of the new visitors are local day-trippers who bring their own food and drink.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: twice the visitors, less spending in town. If the new visitors are day-trippers who bring their own food, and they displace overnight guests in the town's hotels, the mix changes: more visitors but less spending: (E).

(A) concerns the past fee level, not spending. (B) concerns litter. (C) is a standing fact about the town. (D) says the new visitors are local but doesn't say that they spend less in town or that the old ones spent more.
questions.tip: A rise in visitors need not raise spending if the type of visitor changes.
questions.trap: (D) hints at who the new visitors are, but it doesn't link them to lower spending.

questions.prompt:
A shipping company introduced a new route that is 20% faster than its old route. Yet the company's average delivery time per parcel did not improve.

Each of the following, if true, helps to explain why the average delivery time did not improve EXCEPT:
choices: Most of a parcel's journey time is spent waiting in the company's sorting depots, not travelling.
Customers can now track their parcels online.
The new route is used for only a small share of the company's parcels.
Parcels now take longer to be loaded onto vehicles at the start of the new route.
The new route tends to be used for the company's heaviest parcels, which are slow to process.
questions.explanation:
Four choices give a reason why a faster route needn't speed up the average parcel. The exception does not.

(B) is the exception: online tracking does not change how long parcels take, so it explains nothing. (A) shows that the road is not where time is lost. (C) means few parcels benefit. (D) adds loading time that offsets the gain. (E) says the route's parcels are slow to process, offsetting the speed gain.
questions.tip: On EXCEPT questions, a choice that is irrelevant to the puzzle is as good an answer as one that makes it worse.
questions.trap: (E) can look odd, but it is a real offsetting factor; the exception is the one with no bearing on delivery time.

questions.prompt:
In the city of Arvand, the unemployment rate fell from 8% to 6% over the past two years. Yet over the same period, the number of employed residents of Arvand also fell.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The population of Arvand rose over the period.
Wages in Arvand rose over the period.
Many new businesses registered in Arvand over the period.
Many residents left the labour force, by retiring, moving away or giving up their search for work, which shrank the pool of unemployed residents by more than it shrank employment.
The government of Arvand extended unemployment benefits during the period.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: a lower unemployment rate normally means more people working, but employment fell. The rate is unemployed divided by the labour force. If many people left the labour force, the unemployed count (and the labour force) shrank faster than employment, so the rate fell even though employment did too: (D).

(A) and (C) suggest more jobs, deepening the puzzle. (B) concerns pay, not numbers of workers. (E) would encourage people to stay unemployed, raising the rate rather than lowering it.
questions.tip: A rate can fall because its denominator shrank, not because the outcome improved.
questions.trap: (A) is natural to pick for a fall in the rate, but a rising population would normally raise employment.

questions.prompt:
In 2023, the average length of sentences handed down for burglary in the city of Haldia was shorter than in 2022. Yet every individual judge in Haldia handed down longer average burglary sentences in 2023 than in 2022.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The number of burglaries in Haldia fell between 2022 and 2023.
The maximum sentence for burglary in Haldia was raised in 2023.
In 2023, a larger share of burglary cases than in 2022 were heard by the judges who, on average, hand down the shortest sentences.
More judges were appointed in Haldia in 2023 than in 2022.
Sentences for other crimes in Haldia were longer in 2023 than in 2022.
questions.explanation:
Every judge's average rose, yet the city-wide average fell. This is a mix effect: if cases shifted towards the judges with shorter average sentences, the overall average falls: (C).

(A) concerns the number of burglaries, not sentence length. (B) would push sentences up and deepen the puzzle. (D) concerns the number of judges, which doesn't change the mix on its own. (E) concerns other crimes.
questions.tip: When every subgroup rises and the whole falls, the group mix must have shifted.
questions.trap: (D) hints at mix changes but says nothing about where the cases went.

questions.prompt:
In the six months after a streaming service introduced a cheaper, ad-supported subscription tier, its total number of subscribers rose by 20%. Yet its total subscription revenue fell over the same period.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many existing subscribers on the premium tier switched to the cheaper tier, and the revenue lost from these switchers exceeded the revenue from new subscribers.
Advertising revenue from the cheaper tier is not counted as subscription revenue.
The cheaper tier is priced at less than half of the premium tier.
The new subscribers are younger, on average, than the existing subscribers.
Competing streaming services also launched cheaper tiers during the period.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: more subscribers, less subscription revenue. New subscribers on the cheaper tier still add revenue, so something else must subtract more: existing premium subscribers downgrading. If the revenue lost through downgrades exceeded the revenue from new sign-ups, both facts hold: (A).

(B) explains why ad income isn't in the number, but new subscribers would still raise subscription revenue. (C) is the closest wrong choice: a low price explains why new subscribers add little, but they still add something, so revenue shouldn't fall without downgrades. (D) concerns age, which has no clear link to revenue. (E) concerns competitors and gives no reason why this service's revenue would fall.
questions.tip: If something adds revenue, to explain a fall you need a second effect that subtracts more.
questions.trap: (C) explains why new revenue is small but not why total revenue fell.

questions.prompt:
Over the past decade, an investment fund's average annual return was 8%. Yet the average investor in the fund earned only 3% a year on the money they invested in the fund over the same decade.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The fund deducts management fees from the investors' returns before reporting them.
Most of the money invested in the fund came in after years of strong returns, so that most investors' money was invested during the fund's weaker years.
Some investors kept their money in the fund for the entire decade.
The fund's return varied from year to year.
Most of the fund's investors are retired.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle: the fund returned 8% a year, but the typical investor earned 3%. If most money came in after good years, then more money was exposed to the weaker years than to the strong ones, and the money-weighted return that investors actually earned is below the fund's average: (B).

(A) is tempting, but fees deducted before reporting are already in the 8%, so they don't create a gap. (C) is irrelevant, because long-term holders would earn the fund's return. (D) is true of most funds and doesn't create a gap on its own. (E) concerns the investors' age, not their timing.
questions.tip: Averages of returns and returns on the money invested can differ when the amount invested changes over time.
questions.trap: (A) is the classic 'fees' answer, but the passage's 8% figure is already after fees if fees are deducted before reporting.
